A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MaintainCoder and MaintainBench work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and supplied appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original code-generation evaluations across five MaintainBench datasets, initial-code correctness results, and agent ablations in Tables 1–5.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark evaluations, expanded ablations, and additional robustness experiments in Tables 1–6 and Figure 7.

M1.justification: The requirement-analysis, design-pattern selection, framework design/evaluation, and code generation/optimization pipeline is retained. The six agent prompts also match after relocation to Appendix A.2. Newly disclosed iteration limits and construction prompts do not establish a changed underlying method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same five benchmark families and four requirement-change types in Python. The Ext/Dyn terminology is standardized, and entry-level results move to Appendix E; these do not establish different dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V2's benchmark tables add AgentCoder and MapCoder with both backbones, DeepSeek-V3 CoT/Plan variants, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Preview, and Claude-3.5-Sonnet. The initial-code comparison also changes membership: v1's GPT-4o-mini CoT/Planning rows disappear, while GPT-4o and Gemini are added.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluation across k=1–5 and an APPS-Dyn experiment using Gemini-2.5-Flash-Preview as the Phase II modification generator. These extend the testing protocol; the main two-phase evaluation retains GPT-4o-mini and the stated temperature/top-p settings. Newly disclosed iteration limits do not establish revised experimental budgets.

E4.justification: V1's CodeContests-only ablation expands to APPS and xCodeEval in v2 Table 4. V2 also adds generator and Pass@k sensitivity tests, a Pass@5–AST similarity scatter analysis, and a cyclic-array code-output case study. These substantially broaden analysis of component contributions and evaluation sensitivity.

E5.justification: Appendix D newly states that static metrics and dynamic AST/code-change metrics are averaged over five generation rounds. V1 reports Pass@5 without this aggregation detail. This is newly disclosed repetition information, not evidence of increased runs; defined confidence intervals or significance tests are not added.

E6.justification: Corresponding APPS tables revise MaintainCoder Pass@5 from 45.0% to 50.5% with GPT-4o-mini and from 51.5% to 62.5% with DeepSeek-V3. Numerous comparator, ablation, and robustness results are added. The initial-code table also replaces many scores and omits HumanEval/MBPP columns. These are reported result revisions, without an established explanation for every numerical change.

T1.justification: The discounted maintenance-cost formulation, first-step Monte Carlo proxy, and benchmark transformation equations retain their substance after notation/indexing changes. Appendix D supplies the standard formula for the already-used Maintainability Index; it does not introduce new theory or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion replace 14–30% maintainability improvements with claims exceeding 60% for dynamic/post-modification performance. V2 also elevates the claimed consistency and effectiveness of dynamic metrics over conflicting static metrics into a central contribution, and explicitly extends its empirical criticism to evaluated multi-agent systems.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 adds substantive arguments about interpreting maintainability: relative edits better represent maintenance effort, agreement among dynamic metrics supports their validity, and generic multi-agent systems can impair maintainability. It also interprets CoT/Planning effects as inconsistent. V1's qualification that complex design may be unnecessary for simple problems is not retained.

D1.justification: Appendices A, C, and D newly document benchmark-generation and Phase II prompts, annotator qualifications and JSONL review rules, iteration limits of three framework evaluations and five code optimizations, and difflib-based metric computation. Existing agent prompts are relocated. V1's explicit repository link is replaced by anonymous-supplement access statements and a promised public release.

R1.justification: V2 adds maintenance literature, ISO maintenance categories, multi-turn synthesis context, and model references. Section 2 introduces MapCoder, drops ReflectionCoder, and more explicitly distinguishes MaintainBench from SWE-Bench. These refine the existing research positioning around dynamic maintainability.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: Experiments and Results are consolidated, analysis receives a dedicated subsection, and prompts and construction details are reorganized into multiple appendices. Method descriptions are condensed, contributions and conclusions rewritten, and dataset terminology standardized.

P2.justification: The document switches from two-column to single-column formatting. Tables gain backbone groupings, metric-direction arrows, and shaded MaintainCoder rows; prompt figures are paired and relocated. New scatter and Pass@k plots are added. Several new appendix code-listing lines visibly end prematurely at percent signs.

improvement.justification: Matched-backbone multi-agent comparisons, generator-sensitivity testing, and detailed prompts and iteration limits improve assessment and reproducibility. However, stronger claims sometimes exceed the evidence: Section 4.1 claims roughly 60% over the second-best xCodeEval method, while Table 2 gives 36.7% versus 32.8%, about 12%. Figure 7 also does not show universal superiority at small k. These inconsistencies and incomplete appendix code listings limit the net quality gain.
